newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bonds stalled by data-nervous futures.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds stalled by data-nervous futures.

text.p: *Australian bond yields ended well above the day's lows as the future market showed nervousness ahead of key data, both locally and in the U.S., over the next few days.
*Q1 US GDP due later on Wednesday, local AWOTE on Thursday.

Australian bond yields ended well above the day's lows as the futures market showed some nervousness ahead of another set of key U.S. data later on Wednesday and its own first quarter wages report on Thursday.

"Our feeling is that the U.S. will weaken tonight and that our market went a long way on very little. Futures are being very cautious ahead of the figures and there was very little physical flow to back the early rally," one trader said.
Local yields had dropped sharply in early trading, and much in tandem with U.S. Treasuries, which took heart to weaker than expected data on employment costs and durable goods orders.
On the domestic front, the March balance of goods and services proved a non-event for the market, despite showing a A$103 million deficit when median forecasts had centred on a A$150 million surplus.
Economists said the series is proving volatile, and market is more concerned over Thursday's average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) and Friday's retail trade.

First quarter AWOTE forecasts centre on a 0.8 percent rise, bringing annual growth to 4.3 percent and under what is perceived to be the Reserve Bank's 4.5 percent comfort zone, according to a Reuters survey of economists.
March retail trade is seen flat, while the quarterly retail report, due at the same time, is seen rising 2.4 percent.

Weaker than expected outcomes on retail and wages could stir up speculation of a further monetary policy easing given last week's moderate "living wage" case result and a subdued first quarter inflation report.

"Circumsatnces have changed in this last month or so, just in the way the data has panned out. It's benign enough for it (the RBA) to get away with another interest rate cut without damaging its credibility and it helps insurance on the growth side," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.

However, David de Garis, Treasury economist at ANZ Banking Group, expects the retail trade report to be robust enough to kill off any thoughts of an easing and is likely to be a negative for the short-end of the market.

Meanwhile, today's first quarter U.S. GDP is expected to show annual growth at 4.1 percent after 3.8 percent in the fourth quarter last year. The U.S. also faces the April National Association of Purchasing Management index on Thursday followed by non-farm payrolls on Friday.
"That backdrop will have just as large an influence on the bond market than our data," de Garis added.

The local market's caution saw spreads generally widen against the dollar bloc. The largest move was against Canadian debt, which rebounded strongly on Tuesday's U.S. data on the view that the Federal Reserve would be less likely to tighten policy, relieving pressure on Canadian monetary policy.
